verses.1:
Al-Mizan says that this Meccan chapter consoles the Prophet over his people’s denial of him and of the revealed Book, their charges that he was mad or a poet, and their defiance. By recounting the prophets Moses, Abraham, Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shuʿayb and the consequences of their peoples’ denials, it both comforts him and warns his opponents. It is among the early Meccan chapters, apparently revealed before Sūrah al-Ḥijr; reports that its final five verses, or (26:197), were Medinan are to be discussed later.

“Those” in “These are the verses of the clear Book” refers both to this chapter’s verses and those already revealed. The distancing force of tilka indicates their exalted rank, while al-mubīn denotes a Book plainly sent from God through its miraculous qualities, despite the polytheists’ claims that it is devilish inspiration or poetry. In (26:3), bākhiʿ means dying of grief: the Prophet seems close to such grief because they disbelieve in the revealed verses. The wording reproves his harming himself in this way and consoles him.

God could, if He willed, send a heavenly sign that would compel their submission and faith, visibly humbling them as their necks remain lowered. The humbling of the necks is a metonymy for the soul’s humility, outwardly first displayed by lowering the head. Although aʿnāq has been read as groups, as communal leaders, or as requiring an omitted “possessors” of necks, the last reading is least plausible. Instead, their hearts are persistently averse to every renewed reminder of al-Raḥmān; they do not reject a new reminder in preference for old ones. Calling Him the Beneficent indicates that the reminder proceeds from His universal beneficence, the basis of their welfare in this world and the next. Their settled aversion leads to rejection, and their rejection means that the important news, anbāʾ, of what they mock—God’s signs and communications—will soon reach them as punishment in both worlds.

The question about the earth censures them for refusing to reflect on the many beautiful and noble species God has caused to grow. Here yaraw ilā calls for reflective observation, and zawjin karīm may mean diverse plant species, though it may also include animals and human beings, in light of: And Allah has made you grow out of the earth as a growth (71:17). The growth of every noble zawj also displays the pairing through which each mate’s deficiency is completed, guiding species to their intended end and ultimate felicity. It is therefore a sign that the One who guides creation to its good will not neglect to guide human beings to their felicity in this world and the next.

Most nevertheless are not expected to believe, because aversion has become their second nature and has deprived them of the capacity for faith. The Qur’an identifies entrenched moral vice and iniquity as causes of disbelief; thus the verse does not primarily, or by any evidence, refer to God’s foreknowledge of their disbelief. The preceding context instead supports this moral explanation. A report from Sībawayh that kāna is merely connective yields “Most of them are not believers”; though true, this is less suited to the context. God is Mighty and Invincible, and so punishes those who turn from His reminder, reject His signs, and mock His communications; He is Merciful, and so sends guidance, forgives believers, and grants disbelievers respite.

Al-Mizan rejects the determinists’ argument, associated especially with al-Imam al-Rāzī, that God’s eternal knowledge makes human actions necessary and thereby refutes ikhtiyār. Its proponents argue that acts must occur exactly as eternally known, lest divine knowledge be ignorance; when told that knowledge follows its known object, they reply that God’s knowledge follows an event’s māhiyyah, while its external wujūd follows that knowledge. This reply wrongly assumes that quiddity has pre-eternal subsistence and precedence over existence. It also treats God’s knowledge as acquired, conceptual knowledge like ours, whereas things are known to Him directly and presentially: before their existence by knowledge identical with His Essence, and after it by knowledge identical with their very existence.

Moreover, eternal knowledge concerns each event as it will occur with all its characteristics and conditions. A voluntary act is known precisely as an act performed freely by a particular subject, not as an unspecified act; otherwise no determinate external event is being known. Its necessary occurrence is therefore necessary as voluntary, just as something contingent in itself may be necessary through another. The determinist argument confuses an unconditional action with an action qualified by free will, and cannot make divine knowledge strip a known voluntary act of volition. If God knows a voluntary act, it necessarily occurs voluntarily; if He knows an involuntary act, it occurs involuntarily. Finally, were (26:8) saying that pre-eternal knowledge made belief impossible, the disbelievers would have invoked that as an excuse against the Prophet, as some determinists themselves acknowledge; no such argument is reported.

verses.3: Al-Mizan explains bākhiʿ as dying of grief: the Prophet appears close to dying because his people do not believe in the revealed verses of the Book. The verse gently reproves his doing this to himself and is meant to console him.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that the omitted object of “If We willed” is supplied by the clause about sending down a sign: if God willed to send a heavenly sign that compelled submission and faith, He would do so. Their necks would remain lowered in visible humility; attributing humility to necks is a metonymy, since inward humility first appears outwardly in the lowered head. While aʿnāq has been interpreted as groups, communal leaders, or, with an implied possessive, the possessors of necks, the last interpretation is least plausible.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the verse describes their persistent denial: aversion to God’s remembrance is rooted in their hearts, so they turn away whenever a renewed reminder calls them to Him. It means that they reject every reminder that comes, not that they prefer older reminders to a new one. Calling God al-Raḥmān indicates that this reminder issues from His universal beneficence, which secures their welfare in this world and the next.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains that their persistent aversion to every reminder results in their rejection of the truth, and that rejection in turn brings the promised news, anbāʾ, of what they mock. This important news concerns the signs and communications they ridicule: punishment that will soon overtake them in this world and the next.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes the verse as a censuring question: despite their rejection of the signs, do they not reflect upon the many noble species God has caused to grow from the earth? Yaraw ilā here means reflective observation, and zawjin karīm denotes beautiful, splendid, or noble species. It may refer to the diverse plant species, though some extend it to animals and human beings, citing: And Allah has made you grow out of the earth as a growth (71:17).
verses.8:
Al-Mizan says that the sign lies in the growth of every noble zawj: through pairing, each mate’s imperfection is completed by the other, and every species is guided to its intended end and ultimate felicity. The One who thus guides creation cannot neglect to guide human beings to their good in this world and the next.

Most are not expected to believe because ingrained aversion has become their second nature and left them unable to believe. The Qur’an repeatedly identifies entrenched moral vice and iniquity as causes of disbelief and wrongdoing. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the view that the verse primarily refers to God’s foreknowledge of their disbelief: the wording provides no evidence for it, while the preceding verses positively point to their deep-rooted aversion. A narration from Sībawayh treats kāna as a merely connective addition, giving the true sense “Most of them are not believers” (mā aktharuhum muʾminīn), but Al-Mizan finds its own explanation more congruent with the context.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that God’s might means that He punishes in this world and the next those who turn from His reminder, reject His signs, and mock His communications. His mercy means that He sends reminders to guide them, forgives believers, and grants disbelievers respite.

The commentary then rejects the determinists’ argument, recurrent especially in al-Imam al-Rāzī, that God’s pre-eternal knowledge makes all human actions compulsory and invalidates ikhtiyār. They argue that acts must necessarily occur as eternally known, lest divine knowledge become ignorance. In answer to the objection that knowledge follows its known object, they claim that eternal knowledge follows an event’s māhiyyah, while the event’s external wujūd follows that knowledge.

Al-Mizan finds this argument invalid. It wrongly presupposes a pre-eternal subsistence and precedence of māhiyyah over wujūd. It also treats divine knowledge as acquired conceptual knowledge like ours, whereas God knows things directly and presentially: before their existence by knowledge identical with His Essence, and after their existence by knowledge identical with the things’ existence itself.

God’s eternal knowledge concerns an event as it will occur, with every characteristic and condition. Thus, when its object is a voluntary act by a particular subject, it is known as voluntary, not as an unspecified act; indeterminate acts are not externally actualized. The act must consequently occur through the subject’s free choice, since its occurring compulsorily would contradict what God knows. What is necessary is not an unconditional act, but an act qualified by its voluntary character—like something contingent in itself that is necessary through another. The determinists therefore confuse an unconditional action with an action qualified by free will. Divine knowledge of a voluntary act necessitates that it occur voluntarily, just as knowledge of an involuntary act necessitates its involuntary occurrence.

Finally, Al-Mizan notes that, were “but most of them were not believers” (26:8) intended to mean that divine foreknowledge made their faith impossible, the disbelievers would have used this as an excuse against the Prophet. As some determinists admit, no such argument is reported.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains that God’s call commissioned Moses to go to Pharaoh’s people to save the Children of Israel. Calling them “the unjust people” before identifying them as Pharaoh’s people shows why a messenger was sent: they were unjust through polytheism and through tormenting the Israelites. The third-person wording, “Will they not guard (against evil)?”, is a rebuke delivered in their absence: Moses is to convey that God censures their abandonment of taqwā (self-restraint, Godwariness).

verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses feared Pharaoh’s people would accuse him of lying. Majmaʿ al-Bayān defines khawf as disturbance at the expectation of harm, though in ordinary usage it commonly denotes cautiousness in the face of evil whether or not agitation occurs; unlike khashyah, it need not imply inward anxiety. Thus prophets may be described as having khawf, although they have no khashyah of anyone besides God.

Under the usual reading, Moses gives three grounds for asking that revelation be sent to Aaron: fear of rejection, constriction of the breast, and ineloquence of the tongue. Under the reading of Yaʿqūb and others, the latter two follow from his one fear of rejection, a sense also consistent with the account in Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ. To “send to Aaron” means to send the angel of revelation to him so that Aaron may aid in conveying the message.

The commentary stresses that Moses was not evading his own mission. He sought Aaron’s appointment as a messenger to assist him and testify to his truthfulness. Rūḥ al-maʿānī observes, and Al-Mizan accepts, that placing this request amid Moses’ concerns, before his further fear of being slain, shows that it was not a resignation from responsibility.

verses.14: Al-Mizan takes the “claim” (dhanbun) to refer to Moses’ killing of a man. Al-Rāghib says dhanb originally concerns taking something by its tail and thus denotes an act followed by an undesirable consequence. The killing was a dhanb by Pharaoh’s people’s judgment, or in this lexical sense, but the verse provides no evidence that it was a sin of disobedience toward God.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that kallā negates Moses’ fear that they would kill him and gives him security. The command, “So go, both of you,” implicitly grants his request concerning Aaron; its conjunction means that, since they cannot kill Moses, the two should go with God’s signs without fear.

The plural in maʿakum includes Moses, Aaron, and the people to whom they are sent, not Moses and Aaron alone, since the surrounding verbs use the dual. God’s being “with” them means His present, attentive hearing of the exchange between the two messengers and Pharaoh’s people, as in “I do hear and see” (20:46).
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that Moses and Aaron are to tell Pharaoh that they are messengers from the Lord of all realms and demand that he release the Children of Israel. Rasūl appears in the singular either because each is a messenger or because they bear one shared message; some also take it as an infinitive, meaning that they are bearers of the divine message.

“Send with us the Children of Israel” expresses their liberation. It is phrased as sending because, once freed, they were to return to the Holy Land ordained for them, the land of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Pharaoh’s question about having raised Moses is a censuring challenge to his claim of messengership: he claims to know Moses’ origin and life among them and therefore treats this mission as implausible.

verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh’s vague reference to “that deed” magnifies its atrocity; it means Moses’ killing of the Egyptian (Qibṭī) man. In context, kufr means ingratitude for favors, not disbelief. Pharaoh regarded Moses—an Israelite whom he had spared and raised—as a slave indebted to him; Moses’ killing of one of Pharaoh’s people was therefore, in Pharaoh’s view, both disruption of his kingdom and ingratitude for his supposed favors to the Israelites.

Thus Pharaoh challenges Moses’ messengership by recalling his upbringing, the killing, and Moses’ alleged status as an ungrateful Israelite slave. Interpretations that make kufr denial of Pharaoh’s divinity, disbelief in God, or merely ingratitude for a personal favor to Moses do not fit this context.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan reads Moses’ reply as answering Pharaoh’s three objections in a reordered sequence: first the killing, then the supposed implausibility of Moses’ messengership given his past, and finally Pharaoh’s claim of favor. Idhan means “at the time when,” and taʿbīd means enslavement.

“I did it then while I was one of those who were astray” answers the charge concerning the killing. The continuation, “So I fled from you when I feared you; then my Lord granted me judgment,” shows that ḍalāl means ignorance of the right course in contrast to ḥukm: sound judgment concerning realities, good and evil, and the firm ability to act accordingly. Moses defended one who sought his aid without knowing that the man would die or that this would lead to flight from Egypt and years away in Midian. The view that ḍalāl means imprudence is rejected because it makes Moses confess crime and sin, contrary to the prior gift of judgment and knowledge mentioned in Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ. The view that it means love for God neither fits the context nor accords with Qur’anic style. Suggestions that it means unintended action, ignorance of divine law, or forgetfulness can be reduced to the accepted meaning of ignorance.

The conjunction in Moses’ flight indicates that he fled because of the killing and fear of being slain. The apparent difference between this passage, which mentions ḥukm after the incident, and Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ, which mentions it before, is resolved by the indefiniteness of ḥukm: Moses received distinct degrees of judgment before the killing, after his flight, and after Pharaoh’s drowning, until its completion with the Torah. This growth is compared to the development from sound fiṭrah, through mature intellect and self-management, to taqwā as a second nature. Accordingly, ḥukm here is not prophethood: neither language nor context supports that view, and the Qur’an elsewhere distinguishes ḥukm from prophethood.

“And He made me one of the messengers” answers Pharaoh’s challenge that Moses’ known upbringing made messengership unlikely. The commentary infers that messengership is not an acquired status reached through ordinary prerequisites; God grants it, just as He grants judgment. It therefore rejects the view that Pharaoh’s earlier question was simply a reproach for the favor of raising Moses: that reading disrupts the sequence of Moses’ answers, leaves the statement about messengership superfluous, and makes verse (26:22) an unsuitable response.

“And is it a favor you remind me of—that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?” is a negating rhetorical question. Pharaoh’s alleged favor and guardianship over Moses and the Israelites arise only from oppressive enslavement; an oppressor cannot count such authority as beneficence, for that would make slavery itself a favor. The verse names enslavement as the cause but intends its effect, Pharaoh’s resulting authority over them.

The commentary rejects attempts to make the verse mean that Pharaoh favored Moses by not enslaving him, to posit an omitted interrogative hamzah, or to say that enslavement annulled the favor of Moses’ upbringing: these lack textual evidence or remain incomplete. The suggestion that Moses’ being cast into the water and raised by Pharaoh ultimately resulted from Israelite oppression may be true, but the issue is whether the wording establishes it. The claim that Pharaoh merely ordered Moses’ Israelite mother and others to rear him is even farther from the text.

verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that, after failing to discredit Moses’ messengership, Pharaoh questions the One who sent him: “And what is the Lord of all realms?” The question concerns the reality and meaning of this description, not whether God exists. Polytheists acknowledged a singular Necessary Existent beyond full comprehension, but, regarding direct worship of Him as impossible, sought nearness through angels, jinn, purified human saints, and sometimes kings. They regarded these beings as lords governing particular affairs or realms, while Allah was the God of gods and Lord of lords. verses.30: Al-Mizan explains that Moses’ “something manifest” is a sign that makes his claim to messengership evident. A prophetic call has two aspects: the claim to bear a mission from God, which a miracle verifies, and the divine teachings preached, such as God’s unity and the hereafter, which rational arguments establish. Moses therefore asks whether Pharaoh would still imprison him even if he produced a clear proof of his mission.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh answers Moses’ implied claim to possess clear proof by demanding that he produce it, if he is truthful in claiming to have such a sign.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan identifies Moses’ rod becoming an obvious thuʿbān—a giant snake whose reality could not be doubted—and his hand appearing white when drawn from the opening of his bosom as the two signs given to him on Mount Ṭūr.

Pharaoh had hoped for a disputable proof, but the signs could not be ignored, so he accused Moses of skillful magic. By claiming that Moses wished to expel the people from their land, he sought to provoke the chiefs into conspiring against him. “What is it then that you advise?” most likely asks their counsel on how Pharaoh should proceed, since he regarded himself as their highest lord; the same wording elsewhere likewise means advice to Pharaoh. Alternatively, the signs may have so stunned him that he helplessly asked them to command him what to do.

verses.49: Al-Mizan explains that “before I gave you permission” means “without my permission,” not that Pharaoh’s permission was ever expected. Pharaoh falsely alleges that Moses was the magicians’ chief and teacher in order to turn his people, especially the chiefs, away from him. “So you shall know” is an intentionally vague threat, followed by the specified punishment: amputation of the right arm and left leg, or the reverse, and taṣlīb, crucifixion.
verses.50: Al-Mizan explains that ḍayr means harm or loss. The magicians say Pharaoh’s threatened punishment will not harm them because they will endure it and return to their Lord—a noble return.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains that the magicians are not only unafraid of Pharaoh’s punishment and death but eager to return to their Lord. They hope that, as the first to believe in Moses and Aaron, He will forgive their wrongs. Those who first open a path of good for others have a share in that good; thus divine forgiveness and mercy granted for faith will not miss those who first entered and opened that path.
verses.52: Al-Mizan explains that this begins the second part of Moses’ story: the punishment of Pharaoh’s people after their rejection, following the account of the mission and call to monotheism. Asri bi-ʿibādī commands Moses to journey by night with the Children of Israel, whom “My servants” honors by attributing them to God. Their pursuit by Pharaoh’s people is part of the divine purpose: it provides the Israelites respite and leads the pursuing host to its drowning.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains that, after Moses departed at night with the Children of Israel, Pharaoh sent heralds through his cities to mobilize the people. They portrayed the Israelites as an especially small remnant who had angered them, while Pharaoh’s side was a united yet vigilant multitude, fearing possible harm or plotting even from this weak group. This rhetoric was meant to rouse the people against Israel.

God turned Pharaoh’s people out of their gardens, springs, treasures, and fine dwellings through His plan in response to their pride, and the Children of Israel inherited these possessions after Pharaoh and his army were drowned. Kadhālika means “that was the case.”

Pharaoh’s host caught up with the Israelites near sunrise. When the two groups saw one another, Moses’ companions feared they would be overtaken. Moses’ answer, “By no means; surely my Lord is with me,” means that God was present with him in protection and support, not merely present as Creator and Director, a togetherness shared even by Pharaoh. God would guide him to an escape beyond Pharaoh’s reach.

God then commanded Moses to strike the sea with his staff. It split into separate parts, each like a great mound, opening a route for Moses and his companions. God brought Pharaoh and his hosts near to that place, preserved the sea’s divided state until Moses and all with him crossed, and then poured it over the others and drowned them.

verses.67:
Al-Mizan explains that “this” encompasses Moses’ appointment, his call to Pharaoh and his people, the Israelites’ rescue, and Pharaoh’s drowning. The whole story is a sign of God’s unity in lordship and of the truth of the message for those who reflect. “Most of them were not believers” apparently refers to the people in that story despite the clear signs, not directly to the Prophet’s people.

The recurring conclusion after each prophetic story connects these earlier peoples with the Prophet’s community: most people likewise failed to believe when messengers called them to God’s unity in lordship. It consoles the Prophet, telling him not to grieve over their rejection.
verses.68: Al-Mizan states: It repeats the exposition at 26:9.
verses.69: Al-Mizan explains that the command to “recite” Abraham’s story addresses the Arab polytheists, especially the Quraysh, since Abraham was their forefather and stood for monotheism and the true religion. Though none of his contemporaries believed in the declaration that there is no god but God, he aided God and was aided by Him until monotheism was established in the Holy Land and Hijaz. Called both by God and by his unadulterated fiṭrah, Abraham is a lesson for the Meccan polytheists: they should renounce idolatry, as he renounced his father and his father’s people.
verses.70: Al-Mizan states that Abraham had distinct debates with his father and his people, but this concise account combines their shared elements. His question, “What do you worship?” asks after the reality of their gods while adopting the stance of one unfamiliar with them, a debating method that draws opponents into stating their own position and proof. Having only just left his cave and entered his father’s community, Abraham had not previously witnessed their worship; he argued from his pure, unadulterated nature.
verses.71: Al-Mizan reads “so we shall be their votaries” (26:71) as consequence: their continuous adherence to the idols for their own sake results from worshipping them. Because supposedly immaterial angels and jinn were hard to apprehend, worshippers fashioned material figures of their spiritual qualities; star worship similarly treated celestial bodies, or images of their powers when the stars were inaccessible, as representations of their spirits, and saints too received idols. Yet devotion ultimately fixed on the image itself, or at most on its nondivine “lord,” never God. This disproves the claim that an idol is merely a qiblah like the Kaʿbah: Muslims direct their faces to the qiblah while worshipping its Lord, whereas idolaters directed both face and worship to the idol. Abraham therefore presses “We worship”: an object worshipped for itself should hear its callers and confer benefit or avert harm, but inert idols do neither.
verses.72: Al-Mizan explains that Abraham’s rhetorical questions raise two objections to idols. Worship manifests the worshipper’s humility and need, and calling upon a god requires that it know and hear the call; inanimate idols do not hear. People also worship in hope of benefit or protection from harm, yet idols can neither confer benefit nor avert loss. He frames both points as questions so that the idolaters must acknowledge them themselves.

verses.74: Al-Mizan holds that, rather than answer Abraham’s questions negatively and thereby undermine idolatry, the idolaters appealed to the practice of their fathers. They offered no proof beyond blind following (taqlīd). The wording, “We found our fathers doing so,” rather than specifically worshipping, exposes their ignorance of anything beyond inherited outward acts and forms.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains that once Abraham’s opponents had shown that blind adherence to their fathers was their only basis for idolatry, he dissociated himself from them, their idols, and their forefathers. “Have you then considered” follows from this lack of proof: worship founded only on imitation is false and baseless, and those idols are his enemies because their worship harms his religion and soul. Mentioning their ancient fathers denies that long historical practice can turn falsehood into truth or truth into falsehood.

The pronoun in “Surely they are enemies to me” is normally used for intelligent beings, but is applied to the idols because their worshippers treated them as beings possessing intelligence and understanding. “But not the Lord of the worlds” is a disconnected exception: the idols are enemies to Abraham, whereas the Lord of the worlds is not included among them.

verses.78:
Al-Mizan maintains that these verses continue Abraham’s declaration that the Lord of the worlds is not his enemy. They describe God as compassionate and caring, the source of every good and protector from every evil, rather than beginning a new topic.

God’s creation of Abraham proves that He directs Abraham’s affairs, since creation and direction are inseparable: a being that gradually comes to exist and perfection cannot be created by one agent and directed by another. Thus, “so He shows me the way” makes divine guidance consequent upon creation. Apparently this guidance is absolute and continual, embracing worldly and otherworldly good; food, drink, healing, death, and renewed life are particular instances of this universal guidance. It is also possible that “guidance” means religious guidance specifically, in which case it is mentioned first because it is the greatest blessing after existence.

Food, drink, and healing represent the material bounties through which God meets worldly needs. Abraham says, “when I am sick,” because sickness is the absence of bounty and is mentioned only to introduce healing; it is not merely a courtesy by which he avoids attributing sickness to God. The repeated “He Who” makes each attribute an independent proof that God is the Lord who directs Abraham, watches over him, and answers his calls. Death is not annihilation but a transition from one abode to another, and giving life means life after death.

Apparently this guidance is absolute and continual, embracing worldly and otherworldly good; food, drink, healing, death, and renewed life are particular instances of this universal guidance. It is also possible that “guidance” means religious guidance specifically, in which case it is mentioned first because it is the greatest blessing after existence.

Food, drink, and healing represent the material bounties through which God meets worldly needs. Abraham says, “when I am sick,” because sickness is the absence of bounty and is mentioned only to introduce healing; it is not merely a courtesy by which he avoids attributing sickness to God. The repeated “He Who” makes each attribute an independent proof that God is the Lord who directs Abraham, watches over him, and answers his calls. Death is not annihilation but a transition from one abode to another, and giving life means life after death.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains yawm al-dīn as the Day of Resurrection, the day of recompense and retribution. Abraham says “I hope” for forgiveness, unlike his certain statements about divine creation, provision, death, and resurrection, because forgiveness is solely God’s munificence: God has undertaken to guide, provide for, cause death, and restore life, but has not decreed forgiveness for every sinner.

Abraham’s “mistakes” cannot mean disobedience to God’s authoritative commands, since he is an infallible prophet. Mistakes and sins vary with the servant’s rank: for one such as Abraham, they are occasions when necessities such as sleep, eating, and drinking prevent complete absorption in the pure remembrance of God, though these acts are also obedience from another perspective. This accords with his being purified for remembrance of the final abode.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan explains that, after recounting God’s continuous and comprehensive favors from creation through eternity, Abraham is moved to express his servantly need and turns from third-person description to direct supplication. By saying “My Lord,” rather than only “Lord of the worlds,” he invokes the divine care and mercy that answer his request.

Ḥukm means sound understanding and judgment in true beliefs and right action, together with acting accordingly. It includes revelation of true belief and righteous deeds, summarized as tawḥīd and taqwā, and a strengthening revelation that establishes practical righteousness. Its indefinite form conveys exaltation and emphasis.

To be joined with the ṣāliḥīn is to be joined with those possessing goodness of essence, not merely those who perform good deeds. Ṣalāḥ is the opposite of corruption: remaining in accord with one’s original nature so that its proper benefits result without corruption. Essential goodness is full receptivity to God’s mercy, good, and felicity, uncorrupted by false belief or evil action. It follows necessarily from the bestowal of ḥukm, though ḥukm is more specific; Abraham thus asks for ḥukm and for its fruition in essential goodness.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains “a tongue of truthfulness” as a tongue belonging exclusively to truth and speaking only what it truly contains. Abraham apparently asks that God raise among his descendants one like himself, who will uphold his call and summon people to monotheism. It therefore means the continuation of a prophet’s call after his death through messengers like him.

Some identify this with the Prophet’s messengership, citing the report, “I am what my father Abraham asked for,” and the Qur’an’s description of his religion as Abraham’s religion (millata Ibrāhīm). Others take it as Abraham’s enduring good reputation. Al-Mizan holds that neither mere “good remembrance” nor identification with Abraham and Ishmael’s supplication for a messenger is the apparent meaning of the expression.
verses.85: Al-Mizan refers the meaning of inheriting the Garden, that is, Paradise, to its exposition of: These are they who are the inheritors (23:10).
verses.86: Al-Mizan explains that Abraham asks forgiveness for his father in fulfillment of his promise to pray for him. The supplication may have been made while his father was still alive, since Abraham later disavowed him only after it became clear that he was God’s enemy. Accordingly, kāna, “was,” may refer to his father’s prior misguidance and does not establish that he had died when Abraham prayed for him.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan explains khizy as being abandoned by one whose support is expected. Abraham’s plea not to be disgraced when people are raised shows that the terrors of the Resurrection require God’s aid and support. “The day on which property will not avail, nor sons” remains part of Abraham’s speech, apposed to the day of resurrection, rather than being a new divine speech.

Wealth and children assist people through socially constructed relations and means in worldly life, but on the Day of Resurrection realities are unveiled and ties severed. Neither possessions nor kinship will help by virtue of being one’s wealth or children. Their negation therefore extends to every conventionally effective worldly means—such as knowledge, skill, or beauty—and signifies the collapse of social institutions and their established causal powers.

“Except for one who comes to Allah with a sound heart (from evil)” is a disconnected exception: although worldly means do not avail, one who comes to God with a sound heart will be availed by it. A sound heart is a soul free from the stain of iniquity, including polytheism and sins. Thus it, rather than worldly possession or family, is the criterion of success.

Al-Mizan rejects readings that make the exception connected, whether by supplying an omitted possessor of wealth and children or treating soundness of heart as a kind of wealth. Such readings restrict the statement to those who possessed wealth or children, leaving others unaddressed, contrary to the context; another proposed disconnected reading unnecessarily supplies an omitted noun. It also rejects the view that these verses establish Abraham’s biological descent from Āzar and make his prayer for forgiveness merely a prayer for Āzar’s faith, holding that the Qur’an explicitly refutes that premise. On the disconnected reading, joined with “And they do not intercede except for him whom He approves (21:28),” the verse supports the conclusion that Abraham prayed before his father’s death.

verses.105:
Al-Mizan explains that qawm originally denotes a group of men rather than women, although Qur’anic usage generally includes both. Its feminine verb may be due to qawm’s sense of jamāʿah, though some regard qawm as feminine or as usable with either gender.

Although Noah’s people rejected only him, their rejection is attributed to “the messengers” because all messengers bring one monotheistic message: rejecting one is rejecting them all. This is more plausible than the view that the plural merely denotes a genus, though both analyses apply to the similar statements concerning ʿĀd and Thamūd.
verses.106: Al-Mizan explains that Noah is called their “brother” as their relative, and that the question is an admonition to guard against evil.
verses.107: Al-Mizan explains that Noah calls himself trustworthy because he is God’s messenger and conveys only what his Lord has commanded him to convey.
verses.108: Al-Mizan says Noah commands them to fear Allah and obey him because obedience to him is obedience to God.
verses.109: Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s refusal of reward shows that his call serves no worldly interest: he sincerely seeks his people’s good and neither betrays nor deceives them. This requires their obedience. Calling God “the Lord of the worlds” explicitly affirms monotheism and denies the other gods they worshipped in the various realms.
verses.110: Al-Mizan explains that the command is repeated because each of Noah’s qualities—trustworthiness and seeking no reward—independently requires that they obey him.
verses.111: Al-Mizan explains that al-ardhalūn, the plural of ardhal, means those considered low and abased because of their menial occupations. Noah’s opponents measured honor by wealth, children, and servants, and thus disparaged the slaves, poor, and workers whom the rich and elite avoided.
verses.112: Al-Mizan explains that mā is a rhetorical question, though some take it as a negative particle with an omitted predicate. Either way, Noah says that he has no knowledge of what the believers did before they believed.
verses.113: Al-Mizan explains that “my Lord” means the Lord of the worlds who appointed Noah as messenger. “If only you could perceive” is an independent clause, meaning that they lack perception, not a conditional statement as some exegetes suggest. Noah neither knows nor must investigate the believers’ past deeds; their account belongs exclusively to his Lord, who will reward them according to their actions.
verses.114: Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s sole task is to call and plainly warn; therefore, he will not drive away those who turn to him in faith or investigate their former deeds. Their reckoning belongs only to his Lord, the Lord of the worlds.

verses.117: Al-Mizan explains that Noah appeals to God for a resolution after his people have definitively settled on denying him, leaving no hope that they will accept his call.

Noah thus asks for a punishment that destroys only the evildoers and delivers the believers. Some instead take fatḥ directly to mean judgment and decree.

verses.123:
Al-Mizan introduces ʿĀd as an ancient Arab tribe of the Aḥqāf, the “sand-dunes,” whose advanced civilization, fertile land, and pleasant dwellings did not prevent their rebellion, rejection of God’s messengers, and ingratitude. God therefore destroyed them with a destructive wind, obliterating their buildings and works. It has been said that ʿĀd was their forefather’s name, as tribes may be named after an ancestor. The reason for speaking of their rejection of “the messengers,” although they apparently rejected one messenger, was explained in the account of Noah.

Hūd called them to fear God, obey him as a trustworthy messenger, and recognize that he sought no reward except from the Lord of the worlds. Al-Mizan cites an exegete who observes that the five stories in the chapter that begin this way establish the shared basis of messengership: calling people to know God and follow what brings reward and averts punishment. Prophets agreed on this despite time-dependent differences in subsidiary laws, and their freedom from worldly greed is thereby shown. The repeated ending of all seven stories likewise shows that most people reject divine signs, that God is Mighty in punishing deniers, and Merciful in saving believers. A translator’s note explains that the shared opening occurs five times because the stories of Moses and Abraham omit it, whereas all seven retain the shared ending.

Hūd reproached ʿĀd for building monuments or towers on every elevated place merely to display pride and satisfy desire, rather than from need; rīʿ means an elevated land, āyah a sign or monument, and ʿabath futile action. He also blamed their construction of maṣāniʿ—strong castles, fortresses, or tall buildings—as though they expected to live forever; without such a hope of immortality, they would not build what naturally outlasts people. Other proposed readings of these verses are rejected as unsupported by the text or context.

Concerning their violent conduct, Majmaʿ al-bayān defines baṭsh as killing by sword or striking by whip, and jabbār as one who elevates himself over others through power. Jabbār is praiseworthy for God but blameworthy for a servant, since it assumes supreme elevation. Thus, when ʿĀd acted forcefully or fought, they exceeded proper bounds in tyrannical cruelty. Their vain construction, longing for permanence, and tyranny show excess in both appetite (shahwah) and anger (ghaḍab), departing from balance and the limits of servitude. Hūd’s renewed command to fear God and obey him follows from this: they must abandon extravagance and arrogance.

God is described as the One who abundantly supplied them with what they know—cattle, children, gardens, and fountains. Al-Mizan explains that this description itself gives the reason for fearing Him: His bounties require gratitude and their proper, non-extravagant use; ingratitude brings wrath and punishment. The concise mention of abundance is then detailed through those particular blessings. Moreover, they know that these blessings and assistance come from Him alone, without partners in creating or bestowing them; therefore they must worship and thank Him, not idols.

Hūd feared for them the chastisement of a grievous day if they proved ungrateful. Apparently this is the Day of Resurrection, though some exegetes allow that it may be the day of their worldly extermination. Their reply declares that admonition makes no difference to them and leaves Hūd without hope of their faith. By saying that he might not be “one of the admonishers,” rather than merely that he might not admonish them, they emphatically dismiss admonition altogether.

Their statement that this is only a custom (khuluq) of the ancients most likely dismisses Hūd’s call to monotheism and admonition as an old custom of myths and legends. Al-Rāghib distinguishes khulq, inward faculties and traits apprehended by insight, from khalq, outward forms apprehended by sight, though the words share a root. Another possible reading takes “this” to mean their inherited polytheism and idol worship. The proposed interpretation that it means their created existence is simply like that of earlier people, with no resurrection, reckoning, or punishment, is improbable in context. Their further assertion that they will not be punished is thus a denial of the Hereafter, assuming the grievous day refers to Resurrection. They rejected Hūd and were destroyed; this is a sign, though most were not believers, and the Lord is Mighty and Merciful.
verses.124:
Al-Mizan presents Hūd as a trustworthy messenger who calls his people to fear God and obey him, while seeking no reward except from the Lord of the worlds. It cites an exegete who finds this same opening in five stories of the chapter: it shows that messengership essentially calls people to know God and obey what brings reward and averts punishment. The prophets agreed on this foundation despite differences in subsidiary laws across times, and they were wholly free of worldly greed and material motives.

The shared ending of all seven stories—affirming a sign, the disbelief of most people, and the Lord’s might and mercy—shows that most people turn from God’s signs, that He is Mighty in punishing denial, and Merciful in rescuing believers. A translator’s note explains that the common opening appears only five times because the accounts of Moses and Abraham do not contain it, while the common ending appears in all seven.

verses.128: Al-Mizan explains that rīʿ is elevated land, āyah a monument or sign, and ʿabath futile action. verses.129: Al-Mizan defines maṣāniʿ, the plural of maṣnaʿ, as strong castles, solid fortresses, or tall buildings. Their construction is an extension of the preceding blame: ʿĀd made such enduring structures because they hoped to live forever; otherwise they would not build what naturally outlasts human beings. verses.130: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, explains baṭsh as killing with a sword or striking with a whip, and jabbār as one who rises over others and assumes exalted power. Together with the preceding verses, this reveals their transgression through excess appetite (shahwah) and anger (ghaḍab), their abandonment of balance, and their departure from the limits of servitude.
verses.131: Al-Mizan explains Hūd’s command to fear God and obey him as the conclusion from ʿĀd’s excess appetite and anger beyond the bounds of servitude. They must be wary of God and comply with Hūd’s command to abandon extravagance and arrogance.
verses.132:
Al-Mizan explains madd as extending or supplying aid; Al-Rāghib notes that imdād is usually used for desirable support and madd for undesirable increase. God’s description as the One who has abundantly supplied ʿĀd is itself the reason they must fear Him: His cattle, children, gardens, fountains, and all other known blessings require gratitude and proper use without extravagance or arrogance, while ingratitude brings wrath and punishment. The general statement of abundance is then specified through these blessings.

The wording also argues that they know these bounties are God’s aid and gifts, with no partners in their creation or bestowal. Hence God alone, rather than idols, must be feared through worship and gratitude.

verses.151:
Al-Mizan explains that amr, “bidding,” apparently means command, as the opposite of prohibition; some exegetes allow that it means shaʾn, an affair or social course, so that obeying it means following the course the leaders seek for the public. In either case, the extravagant are the society’s chiefs and elite. Ṣāliḥ may be addressing their followers, having despaired of the elite’s belief, or everyone, including the elite themselves, since they followed their forefathers, as shown by: Do you (now) forbid us from worshipping what our fathers worshipped? (11:62).

The extravagant, al-musrifin, transgress truth and the balanced limits. Their mischief and failure to act aright explain why they must not be obeyed: corrupters are not secure from God’s punishment, for He is Mighty and Vengeful.

The commentary grounds this in a rational account of the universe. Although its parts may conflict, they are coordinated toward an end, like opposing pans of a scale that together determine weight. The human world and each human being likewise possess a balanced order: faculties have their due shares, and intellect distinguishes good from evil. Every part follows an appointed middle path; a deviation by excess or deficiency threatens the whole system. Other parts therefore restore the deviating part if possible, or otherwise destroy it to preserve the well-being of the whole.

Human beings are subject to this same order. By following fiṭrah, they attain their appointed felicity; by exceeding its limits and spreading corruption, they incur famine, natural disasters, and other punishments intended to return them to the constructive path, as stated in (30:41). If corruption has become rooted in their hearts and continues, God destroys them with an exterminating punishment. Belief and guarding against evil bring blessings, whereas rejection brings requital; God does not destroy towns tyrannously while their people act well, and His righteous servants inherit the earth (7:96), (11:117), (21:105). Their appropriate actions accord with the universal order, improving the earth and making it more fit for their life.

Thus, Al-Mizan concludes that the prophetic call truly seeks to reform human life on earth—Shuʿayb says, I desire nothing but reform so far as I am able (11:88)—and that Ṣāliḥ’s prohibition of obeying the extravagant rests on rational argument. The added phrase “and do not act aright” perhaps indicates that, though they share human fiṭrah and should act rightly, they have replaced right action with mischief.

Al-dhukrān is the plural of dhakar, male, as opposed to unthā, female; al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam, a group of people. “From among all people” may qualify the implied “you,” reproaching them, among all people, for an act no one had done before them, as in Which no one in the world has ever done before you? verses.166:
Al-Mizan explains tadharūna as “to leave” or “abandon.” The differentiation of human beings into male and female, their organs and faculties, sexual desire, and their active and passive roles show that sexual union is ordered to procreation and the continuance of the species. Thus a man is created for a woman and a woman for a man, establishing the natural wedlock by which they form a pair.

The commentary distinguishes this natural wedlock from marriage as a social convention, which establishes exclusivity and defines its boundaries through social or religious considerations. Since marriage is founded on procreation and reproduction rather than mere partnership in life, human nature leads men to women and women to men, not men to men or women to women.

It is therefore most plausible that “what your Lord has created for you” denotes the female organ made lawful to men through marriage. The lām in lakum indicates a naturally established ownership, while min in min azwājikum is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah): they abandon the part of their wives created and assigned for them. The verse primarily concerns natural marriage, though it may also allude to its social-conventional form. Some exegetes take mā to mean women, with “of your wives” explanatory, but Al-Mizan considers this unlikely.

ʿĀdūn means that they transgress the limits set by creation and nature, equivalent to: What! Do you come to males and accost wayfarers? (29:29). These points show that Lot’s speech contains a latent rational argument. When his people threatened to expel him, al-mukhrajīn meant those expelled from their land, like the reported demand: Turn out Lot’s followers from your town (27:56).

verses.192:
Al-Mizan explains that “this” is the Qur’an, returning to the chapter’s opening description of the clear Book and its subsequent account of those who reject its reminders. Tanzīl and inzāl both mean sending down, though the former usually suggests a gradual act and the latter a sudden one.

For non-physical things, descent is understood in a manner suited to the thing itself. God’s tanzīl is His bringing forth of something from the invisible realm into the realm of creation, measure, and visibility. As the High, Exalted, and All-Dominant, He diffuses things from Himself by creating them in that realm. The Qur’an uses this language not only for revelation but also for clothing, cattle, iron, and, in general, every thing sent down in a known measure. The Qur’an itself is likewise made an Arabic Qur’an though it is, with God, in the elevated and firm original of the Book.

Calling this tanzīl a revelation from “the Lord of the worlds” affirms God’s exclusive Lordship over all worlds, against the polytheists’ acceptance of Him merely as Lord over other lords.
verses.193:
Al-Mizan identifies the Faithful Spirit, al-rūḥ al-amīn, as Gabriel, the angel of revelation. He is called faithful because he conveys God’s message without alteration, disorder, error, or forgetfulness; his description elsewhere as the Holy Spirit conveys the same point. The phrase “has descended with it” means that Gabriel brought the Qur’an down, not merely that he descended in its company.

The Qur’an brought down is a divine speech whose words and letters, no less than its true meanings, are revealed by God. The commentary therefore rejects the view that Gabriel conveyed only meanings which the Prophet subsequently expressed in Arabic, and regards as still weaker the claim that both wording and meaning were composed by the Prophet, with one level of his soul called the Faithful Spirit imparting them to another called the heart.

“Upon your heart” means upon the Prophet’s human soul, not the bodily organ in the chest, since the Qur’an attributes cognition, understanding, will, and sin to the heart. This wording indicates the mode in which he received revelation: his soul encountered the Spirit and received what was revealed without the physical senses of sight and hearing. Narrations concerning buraḥāʾ al-waḥy, the intensity of revelation, confirm that he saw the angel and heard his voice in a manner analogous to ordinary seeing and hearing, but not by bodily senses; people around him could remain unaware while revelation came to him.

To suppose that he perceived these matters through ordinary senses while God simply prevented others from perceiving them would undermine reliance on sensory perception, on which self-evident knowledge and assertion depend, and would rest on the false principle that nothing exists except what is sensible. The commentary similarly rejects explanations that make revelation arrive through bodily hearing and sight, divide the Prophet into angelic and human aspects on this basis, identify the heart with the physical organ, or describe revelation by physical sound, memory, sensory transmission, and imaginative faculties. Such interpretations wrongly measure a transcendent event by familiar physical events. It also rejects the notion that the Prophet became an angel to receive revelation, or that an angel became human, as unintelligible given the supposed separation of their realities.

The purpose of this descent is that the Prophet be among the mundhirīn: callers to God who warn people of His punishment. Indhār is not exclusive to prophets, though the present formulation reflects this chapter’s context of warning and threat. “In plain Arabic language” most fittingly qualifies Gabriel’s descent: he brought the Book down in clear, expressive Arabic, rather than identifying the Prophet merely as one of the Arab warners.

Indhār is not exclusive to prophets, though the present formulation reflects this chapter’s context of warning and threat. “In plain Arabic language” most fittingly qualifies Gabriel’s descent: he brought the Book down in clear, expressive Arabic, rather than identifying the Prophet merely as one of the Arab warners.
verses.196:
Al-Mizan explains that “it” means the Qur’an, or the fact of its revelation to the Prophet, and that zubur is the plural of zabūr, “book.” The verse therefore says that earlier prophets’ books gave news of the Qur’an or of its revelation to the Prophet.

The commentary rejects the interpretation that the pronoun refers merely to the Qur’an’s teachings, such as monotheism and resurrection. The polytheists did not accept former prophets and scriptures such that this would establish an argument against them; whereas a prior prophecy of the Qur’an and its revelation would compel recognition. Moreover, that interpretation does not accord with the following verse.
verses.197:
Al-Mizan explains that what the learned men of the Israelites know is the news of the Qur’an or its revelation to the Prophet, as foretold in earlier prophetic scriptures. Their knowledge is thus a sign sufficient to establish the authenticity of his prophethood for the polytheists.

The Israelites had spoken of this promise and sought victory over the Arabs through it; many of their learned men later embraced Islam and acknowledged that the Prophet had been promised in their books. Since this was an early Meccan chapter, before Jewish hostility reached its later intensity, it was expected that they would disclose at least something of the truth they possessed.
verses.198:
Al-Mizan takes al-aʿjamīn to mean those whose speech is unclear or foreign, rather than requiring the assumption that letters have been omitted from the word. Although the term commonly applies to non-Arabs, an aʿjam is one whose speech lacks clarity, whether Arab or non-Arab.

The verses explain and justify the Qur’an’s descent “in plain Arabic language” (26:195). It was revealed in lucid Arabic so that its Arab audience could understand and believe; had a recited book been revealed to a foreigner in a foreign language, they would have rejected it through failure to understand it. Thus, revelation “to a foreigner” here means revelation in a foreign tongue, as in the analogous statement about a Qur’an in a foreign language.

The commentary rejects an interpretation that imagines an Arabic Qur’an revealed to a non-Arab who miraculously recites it in flawless Arabic, followed by the Arabs’ rejection despite two miracles. That reading fits the theme of obstinate defiance less directly than the connection with plain Arabic speech. The objection that this would mean revealing an Arabic Qur’an in a foreign language is answered by taking al-qurʾān in its literal sense of a recited book, rather than necessarily the specific Arabic Qur’an; the same consideration applies to “Surely We have made it an Arabic Quran that you may understand (43:3).”

verses.200:
Al-Mizan explains sulūk as causing something to enter a path and traverse it. “Thus” refers to the Qur’an’s position in the eyes of the polytheists: despite being revelation from the Lord of the worlds, clear Arabic speech, foretold in earlier scriptures, and known to Israelite scholars, it enters their hearts in a manner that they loathe, turn away from, and disbelieve in it.

They are called “the guilty” because their guilt is the cause of this condition: it is a divine requital for their guilt. The verse directly concerns the Meccan polytheists, but applies generally to every guilty person because the cause is universal.

The commentary considers less likely the view that “thus” refers to the Qur’an’s previously mentioned attributes, so that it enters the guilty hearts with those attributes and thereby completes the proof against them. It regards the interpretation that the pronoun means their implied rejection of the Qur’an as close to its own, but less precise. It also rejects restricting “the guilty” to later or other polytheists, since individual cases may be compared with the universal quality of guilt that includes them; perhaps the expression can encompass both the Meccans and others.
verses.201:
Al-Mizan treats these verses as an elaboration of the Qur’an’s entering the hearts of the guilty, according to the more plausible interpretations of the preceding verse. They persist in unbelief until they behold a painful punishment, when belief is compelled and no longer beneficial. Apparently this punishment is what they witness at death, not the slaughter at Badr, since the statement includes all guilty polytheists.

The punishment comes suddenly while they are unaware; otherwise they could prepare and believe voluntarily before being compelled. Their question, “Shall we be respited?” expresses regret.

verses.208:
Al-Mizan explains that no town is destroyed unless warners have come to it as reminders, thereby completing the proof against its people. The expression “We have not been unjust,” rather than merely “We did not wrong them,” means that injustice never befits God’s station: destruction without prior warning would be unjust, and God is never such as to commit injustice.

Injustice, ẓulm, means acting or disposing without authority or ownership, while justice is acting within one’s possession and jurisdiction. At the level of existence, takwīn, injustice cannot apply to God: all things and their being depend utterly upon Him, and He has absolute ownership of them. Whatever He does to them, whether pleasant or harmful, is therefore not wrong. Created agents possess their acts only through His bestowal, and their possession remains subordinate to His.

Human beings nevertheless possess voluntary choice: each knows that one may act or refrain. Since human life is social, people must forgo acts that disrupt society; laws prohibit such offences, prescribe punishment for transgressors who know the law and have no excuse, and provide reward for those who obey. Enforcement also requires accountable authority, lest the innocent be punished and the guilty released at will, thereby nullifying law itself. Human fiṭrah recognizes these principles.

Rational proof, confirmed by the succession of prophets, shows that God establishes the divinely ordained laws required by fiṭrah for human felicity and social welfare. He is their Legislator and their Executor, rewarding and punishing at the return to Him. In this legislative, tashrīʿī, order—not in the existential order—He has made certain things incumbent upon Himself, so that He does not contradict His own law. He therefore does not neglect every due penalty, punish the ignorant and excused as He punishes the deliberate defiant sinner, or impose the oppressor’s penalty on the oppressed. This is the sense in which God is capable of injustice but certainly does not commit it: injustice is an imperfection from which He is exalted, even though its actual occurrence from Him is impossible. The Qur’anic denial of injustice shows that it is not simply meaningless to speak of injustice in relation to God.

The commentary qualifies this by holding that God may, through grace, remit a sinner’s punishment, but cannot remit punishments without exception, for that would abolish legislation, penal order, and the connection between acts and consequences. Nor does the claim that rewards are pure divine grace negate reward: another divine grace is that God treats the servant’s acts as belonging to the servant and sets reward for them, as the Qur’an repeatedly affirms.

verses.210:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses answer the claim that evil jinn bring the Qur’an to Muḥammad. They are addressed first to the Prophet, to console him, and are linked to the Qur’an’s being revelation from the Lord of the worlds. The argument that devils are far removed from hearing heavenly news is one the unbelievers would not accept; the address then turns toward them in the following verses.

Shayāṭīn here are evil jinn. They have not revealed the Qur’an, nor does doing so befit them: their nature is evil, corruption, and disguising falsehood as truth in order to mislead, whereas the Qur’an is true speech inaccessible to falsehood. Nor are they able to bring it down, for it is a heavenly speech received by angels from the Lord of Glory and conveyed by His leave under His guarding and protection.

The devils are also excluded from hearing what occurs in the exalted assembly. If they attempt to eavesdrop, they are driven away by shining flames; any news they obtain is therefore unavailable or incomplete.

Al-Mizan holds that this command addresses the Prophet. Since the Qur’an is revelation from the Lord of the worlds, not a satanic communication, and since it forbids associating partners with God and threatens punishment for it, he is forbidden to call upon another god with God; otherwise the promised punishment would reach him as it reaches other punished people.

The Prophet’s divinely protected infallibility does not remove commands and prohibitions from him. An infallible person remains a human agent subject to duties and, in itself, capable of obedience or disobedience; the Qur’an gives injunctions to prophets, including warnings that association with God would render deeds ineffectual.

The commentary rejects the notion that injunctions cease after a person has attained perfection. Righteous acts commanded by God are effects of the perfection sought, and one acquires perfection by fulfilling its requirements and avoiding their opposites, then preserves it by continuing to fulfil those same duties. So long as one lives as a human being on earth, one bears injunctions and obligations.
verses.214: Al-Mizan explains ʿashīrah as one’s kin, those with whom one associates. The command to warn the Prophet’s nearest relatives follows the warning addressed to himself against polytheism in order to show that the religious call admits no exception, favoritism, or relaxation of the rule for close relations. There is no difference in warning between the Prophet and his community, or between his relatives and strangers: all are God’s servants and He is their Master.
verses.215: Al-Mizan explains “lower your wings” as a metaphor: the Prophet is to draw the believers who obey him close with mercy and compassion, as a bird gathers its young beneath lowered wings. Here following means obedience.
verses.216: Al-Mizan explains that believers who follow the Prophet are to be gathered and taught with mercy, but if they disobey, he must declare himself free from their deeds.
verses.217:
Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is responsible only for the duty imposed on him, not for whether people obey. He should entrust their case to God, who punishes sinners by His might and saves obedient believers by His mercy.

The names “the Mighty, the Merciful” recall the preceding accounts of Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Abraham, Lot, Shuʿayb, and Pharaoh’s people. Those histories show God’s customary way: He overtakes sinners and saves believers.
verses.218: Al-Mizan takes the apparent meaning to be that God sees the Messenger when he stands in prayer and sees his movement among believers prostrating in congregational prayer. Thus he remains under God’s watch in both standing and prostration. The commentary notes that Shia and Sunni narrations on these verses will be considered separately.

Thus he remains under God’s watch in both standing and prostration. The commentary notes that Shia and Sunni narrations on these verses will be considered separately.
verses.220: Al-Mizan explains that God’s being the Hearing, the Knowing grounds the command to rely on the Mighty, the Merciful. The preceding verses thus console the Prophet, promise salvation to believers, and promise punishment to unbelievers.
verses.221:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses identify the persons upon whom devils descend, thereby refuting the polytheists’ claim that the Prophet receives the Qur’an from them. Devils descend with purported unseen news upon every affāk, an habitual liar who turns truth into falsehood, and athīm, an evil-doer. Since devils themselves adorn evil and disguise falsehood as truth, they only associate with sinful liars.

“They cast their hearing” apparently means that the devils convey what they hear of heavenly news. Yet their eavesdropping is obstructed and they are driven away by shining flames, so whatever they obtain is incomplete and mixed with much falsehood. “Most of them are liars” may mean that most devils are liars, or that most of the revelations brought by those who bring news are lies.

The Prophet is neither a sinful liar nor the recipient of speech that departs from truth. Therefore he is not among those upon whom devils descend, the being who descends upon him is not a devil, and the Qur’an is not a satanic revelation.

Al-Mizan explains that these verses answer the Meccan polytheists’ accusation that the Prophet was a poet, following the answer to their claim that jinn brought him the Qur’an. The repeated Meccan character of both accusations, and the fact that these are the chapter’s concluding verses, confirms that they were revealed in Mecca rather than added in Medina.

Ghayy is the opposite of rushd, arriving at truth. A ghawī pursues falsehood and departs from truth, whereas a rashīd seeks only what is real and true. Poetic art has a special relation to such deviation because it rests on imagination and makes the unreal assume the form of the real. Poets of this kind are followed only by those captivated by illusory attractions and diverted from truth and rectitude.

Their wandering “in every valley” means unrestricted speech with no limit: they may praise false and blameworthy things as true and praiseworthy, vilify what is fair, summon people to falsehood, and turn them from truth. This and their saying what they do not do both depart from the rectitude of fiṭrah.

The Prophet is therefore not a poet in this condemned sense. Such poets are followed by the astray and their art is founded upon error, while the Prophet’s followers seek rectitude and truth because the Qur’an calls to truth and rectitude, not falsehood and error.

verses.227:
Al-Mizan explains that the exception concerns poets: it excludes believing poets from the preceding condemnation. Faith and righteous action restrain them from abandoning truth for falsehood, while abundant remembrance of God makes them mindful of what He approves and turns them away from what He does not. This explains why the exception joins faith and good deeds with frequent remembrance of God.

Their defending themselves after oppression means intiqām, retaliation or revenge. The commentary considers it a sound, contextually supported interpretation that this refers to poems composed by Muslim believers in answer to polytheists who insulted the Prophet, attacked the religion, and disparaged Islam and Muslims.

Those who act unjustly are, in context, the polytheists. They will soon know the munqalab—the place to which they finally return, namely the Fire—or the kind of turning that awaits them. The verse threatens them and returns the chapter to its opening warning that the news of what they mock will come to them.
